reasoning_traces.think:
The core mechanism of voluntary action is rooted in the interplay between neural correlates of movement and antagonistic inhibition. Each sensation triggers neural activity that inherently primes motor output. However, this priming can be blocked by competing representations—antagonistic ideas—that require explicit mental consent (fiat) to override. Motor inertia further complicates this by introducing resistance to initiating movement, especially under conditions of fatigue or disease. These three components form a triadic system where neural activation (F), inhibition (I_a), and inertia (I_m) interact dynamically. When F exceeds both I_a and I_m, action occurs. This framework supports a dual-process model: automatic neural priming and controlled deliberation via fiat. The breakdown regime occurs when any component dominates—either too much inhibition prevents action, or excessive inertia delays it beyond relevance. The system exhibits nonlinearity in its response to inputs, particularly near critical thresholds where small changes in F or I_a can cause large shifts in outcome.
